user_request: Build an AI document intelligence platform using AWS. It should allow users to upload PDF documents, extract text using OCR, store documents securely, provide semantic search and question answering using RAG, support user authentication, and expose APIs for integration with other enterprise systems. Prefer reusable open-source solutions where appropriate, but ensure the selected components have suitable licenses and acceptable security/maturity.
normalized_request: Enterprise AI document intelligence platform enabling PDF upload, OCR-based text extraction, secure document storage, semantic search with RAG-based question answering, user authentication, and REST APIs for third-party integration.

requirements.description: Support secure PDF document upload from authenticated users with validation and virus scanning
Extract text from PDF documents using OCR with support for scanned and digital PDFs
Store documents and extracted metadata securely with encryption at rest and in transit
Enable semantic search across document collections using vector embeddings
Provide question answering capability using RAG to retrieve relevant document sections and generate answers
Authenticate users and manage access control to documents and platform features
Expose REST APIs for document ingestion, search, QA, and system integration with third-party applications
Monitor system health, performance, and usage metrics with observability and logging
Manage user sessions, permissions, and audit trails for compliance and security

risks: CRITICAL: No security audit data provided for evaluated candidates (PDFWorld, EasyOCR, PyMuPDF, LangChain, FAISS, ChromaDB, Keycloak). Deployment must include independent CVE assessment and penetration testing before production.

CRITICAL: LLM vendor selection (OpenAI, Anthropic, open-source Llama) impacts cost (potentially $1000s/month for high-volume QA), data privacy (vendor access to documents via LLM API), and regulatory compliance. Decision must be made upfront with cost modeling and privacy review.
HIGH: PDFWorld relies on AWS S3 backend; on-premises deployments or multi-cloud strategies require architectural rework or alternative storage integration. Verify S3 dependency before commitment.

HIGH: Virus scanning integration (ClamAV or VirusTotal API) adds operational dependency and latency (ClamAV: 2-5s per file, VirusTotal API: subject to rate limits). Plan scanning timeout and fallback handling.

HIGH: EasyOCR accuracy varies significantly by document quality, language, and layout (typical 85-95% for high-quality documents, <70% for poor quality). OCR accuracy benchmark required; establish user expectations and review thresholds for automatic processing.

HIGH: Vector database scaling (FAISS/ChromaDB) has limits. FAISS is in-memory (max ~1M vectors on typical hardware). ChromaDB is persistent but single-node. Plan migration path to cloud vector DBs (Pinecone, Weaviate) at scale (>10M documents).

MEDIUM: Conversational memory in RAG introduces data retention and privacy risks. Multi-turn conversation data must be retained for context but subject to GDPR right to erasure, HIPAA data retention policies. Explicit retention policies and user controls required.

MEDIUM: Keycloak (via user-management-platform) adds operational complexity for federation setup (LDAP, SAML, OpenID Connect). Misconfiguration can introduce privilege escalation or token validation bypasses. Security hardening and audit required.

MEDIUM: Custom COMP-003 and COMP-007 implementations add development and maintenance burden. Audit trail correctness is critical for compliance; inadequate implementation can lead to audit failures or failed incident investigations.

MEDIUM: Prometheus/Loki retention and scalability require careful configuration. Default settings may cause storage exhaustion at high event volumes (>100k events/sec). Plan retention policies and archival strategy.

MEDIUM: API Gateway consumption-based pricing can become expensive at high throughput (>10M requests/month). Requires cost monitoring and budget controls; consider reserved capacity or cost optimization (caching, batching).

MEDIUM: Project health unknown for several candidates: PDFWorld (activity/security status), CAND-016 user-management-platform (Keycloak integration stability), CAND-027 (underlying component versions). GitHub repository evaluation required before commitment.
LOW: Python runtime dependency for OCR and RAG components. If existing stack is non-Python, adds language heterogeneity and deployment complexity. Mitigated by containerization.

LOW: Prompt injection attacks and LLM hallucinations present reputational and liability risks. Adversarial input filtering and source attribution enforcement required; user education on RAG limitations needed.
LOW: Data residency requirements (GDPR, data localization regulations) may conflict with AWS S3/Keycloak deployment. Plan multi-region architecture if required; document data residency compliance.
assumptions: AWS cloud deployment is acceptable; no on-premises or air-gapped environment constraints assumed. If required, alternative storage and compute services must be evaluated.
PDFWorld, EasyOCR, PyMuPDF, LangChain, FAISS, ChromaDB, and Keycloak are considered acceptable as foundational open-source components. Security audit and CVE assessment will validate this assumption.

Virus scanning is assumed achievable via ClamAV (self-hosted) or VirusTotal API integration; neither is included in evaluated candidates but are mature, production-ready services.
Document-level access control can be implemented as a custom RBAC extension layer on top of Keycloak; no specialized identity provider feature assumed.

OCR accuracy of 80-90% is acceptable for initial MVP; documents below confidence thresholds will be flagged for manual review. Accuracy improvement (multi-model ensemble, fine-tuning) deferred to post-MVP optimization.
RAG retrieval context window is limited by LLM token limits (e.g., 4K-100K tokens for OpenAI/Anthropic). Assumption: retrieved chunks fit within context window without truncation or summarization.
Conversational memory is stored in application memory (short-term) and DynamoDB (long-term) with 30-day default retention. Explicit user control for memory clearing supports GDPR right to erasure.
Audit logging volume is assumed manageable (10K-100K events/day); high-volume scenarios (>1M events/day) require data partitioning and archival strategy optimization.
API Gateway traffic is assumed moderate (<1M requests/month) for cost modeling. High-traffic scenarios require cost optimization review and caching strategy.
Third-party integrations via REST APIs assume synchronous request/response patterns. Asynchronous event-driven integrations (webhooks, pub/sub) deferred to future phases.
User adoption and growth is assumed gradual (initial <1000 users, <10k documents). Scaling beyond these thresholds triggers infrastructure optimization review.

Compliance requirements (GDPR, HIPAA, SOC 2) are assumed applicable; implementation prioritizes alignment with these frameworks. Organization-specific compliance (industry, jurisdiction) may require additional hardening.

findings: POSITIVE: Modular microservices architecture is coherent, with clear separation of concerns across ingestion (COMP-001), processing (COMP-002), storage (COMP-003), AI (COMP-004), security (COMP-005, COMP-007), API (COMP-006), and observability (COMP-008). Each component has a well-defined responsibility.

POSITIVE: Data flow follows logical progression: upload → validation → OCR extraction → embedding → vector storage → semantic search/RAG. Integration points are explicitly defined with clear source-target relationships.

POSITIVE: Security architecture layers appropriately: authentication (COMP-005), API validation (COMP-006), document-level access control (COMP-005 extension), audit logging (COMP-007), and encryption (at rest in COMP-003, in transit across boundaries). Layers do not conflict.

CONCERN: COMP-005 is extended with a custom document-level access control layer not fully detailed in the architecture. While the assumption is stated, the implementation complexity and integration with COMP-003 storage queries could introduce consistency issues if not carefully designed. Recommendation: define explicit permission checking API contract between COMP-005 extension and COMP-003/COMP-004.

CONCERN: Vector database scaling assumptions (FAISS/ChromaDB limited to ~1M vectors, migration path to Pinecone/Weaviate) suggest future architectural changes. Current design does not explicitly handle multi-vector-DB deployment or migration orchestration. This is noted as a risk but not addressed in the architecture itself.
POSITIVE: Encryption strategy is consistent: KMS at rest (S3, DynamoDB), TLS in transit (API, component boundaries). Key rotation policies are mentioned for COMP-003.

CONCERN: COMP-004 RAG pipeline assumes LLM vendor will be selected later ('selection during COMP-004 implementation phase'). This defers a critical architectural decision (cost, latency, data privacy implications) to implementation. Current architecture is LLM-agnostic but lacks guidance on vendor decision framework.
POSITIVE: Amazon API Gateway as REUSE decision is architecturally sound; managed service eliminates architectural debt for API layer and reduces operational burden.

CONCERN: Custom BUILD decisions (COMP-003, COMP-007) add implementation complexity. While justified (no suitable candidates), the architecture does not provide sufficient implementation detail (e.g., DynamoDB schema, cryptographic signing approach for audit logs) to validate consistency at implementation stage.

POSITIVE: End-to-end data flow is traceable and logically coherent. Explicit data flow section lists 21 sequential steps from authentication through archival, demonstrating understanding of state transitions.

POSITIVE: Encryption is applied at multiple stages: upload (COMP-001 KMS), storage (COMP-003 S3 SSE-KMS), transit (TLS), and audit logging (COMP-007 HMAC signing). Flow shows no unencrypted sensitive data exposure.

POSITIVE: Access control filtering is integrated into search/QA data flow: COMP-004 retrieves results, then filters via COMP-005 document-level permissions before return. This prevents unauthorized document access.

POSITIVE: Audit event generation is embedded at all critical data flow points (uploads, extractions, searches, QA, auth events). Events flow to both COMP-007 (storage) and COMP-008 (real-time monitoring).

CONCERN: Text chunking occurs in COMP-002 (extraction) but vector embedding and storage in COMP-004 (RAG). No explicit mechanism described for chunk versioning or re-embedding if extraction quality improves. Data consistency between text chunks and vectors could diverge if COMP-002 extraction changes post-embedding.

POSITIVE: Audit event flow to COMP-007 is bidirectional with COMP-008: events are stored in DynamoDB/S3 and streamed to Loki for real-time monitoring. Dual persistence improves auditability.

CONCERN: Cache layer (Redis) is mentioned in COMP-004 implementation notes but not integrated into data flow diagram. Cache hit/miss semantics and invalidation strategy not described. This could introduce data staleness issues for frequently searched documents.
POSITIVE: Archive flow (COMP-003 → S3 Glacier after 90 days) is explicitly mentioned. Retention policy enforcement is clear.
